sunday.themeNote: This week's readings all ask the same quiet question: what are you willing to endure for something true and good? Jeremiah tried to stay silent but couldn't. Paul asks us to stop letting the world around us do all the shaping. And Jesus tells his followers that the path forward runs straight through difficulty, not around it.

readings.label: First Reading
readings.summary: Jeremiah is frustrated. He feels like God pulled him into a role he never asked for, and speaking God's message has brought him nothing but ridicule. He tries to quit, to just stop talking about God altogether. But he finds he can't do it. Something inside him keeps burning, and staying silent feels worse than the mockery.

reflection.reflection: God can put something so deep inside us that we can't stay quiet about it, even when speaking up costs us. That inner fire is worth paying attention to.
reflection.question: Is there something you keep coming back to, a conviction or a value, that feels hard to ignore even when it would be easier to just let it go?

readings.label: Responsorial Psalm
readings.fullText:
R. (2b) My soul is thirsting for you, O Lord my God.
O God, you are my God whom I seek;
for you my flesh pines and my soul thirsts
like the earth, parched, lifeless and without water.
R. My soul is thirsting for you, O Lord my God.
Thus have I gazed toward you in the sanctuary
to see your power and your glory,
for your kindness is a greater good than life;
my lips shall glorify you.
R. My soul is thirsting for you, O Lord my God.
Thus will I bless you while I live;
lifting up my hands, I will call upon your name.
As with the riches of a banquet shall my soul be satisfied,
and with exultant lips my mouth shall praise you.
R. My soul is thirsting for you, O Lord my God.
You are my help,
and in the shadow of your wings I shout for joy.
My soul clings fast to you;
your right hand upholds me.
R. My soul is thirsting for you, O Lord my God.
readings.summary: The psalmist is deeply longing for God, the way someone lost in a desert longs for water. This isn't a polite or distant feeling. It is urgent and physical. But even in that longing, there is trust. The psalmist clings to God and finds real comfort, like someone finally sitting down to a full meal after going hungry.

reflection.reflection: Longing is not the opposite of trust. The psalm shows that aching for something more can actually be the beginning of finding it.
reflection.question: When was the last time you felt a quiet but persistent sense that something was missing? What were you doing, and what do you think you were actually looking for?

readings.label: Second Reading
readings.fullText:
I urge you, brothers and sisters, by the mercies of God,
to offer your bodies as a living sacrifice,
holy and pleasing to God, your spiritual worship.
Do not conform yourselves to this age
but be transformed by the renewal of your mind,
that you may discern what is the will of God,
what is good and pleasing and perfect.
readings.summary: Paul is writing to early Christians in Rome and urging them to make their whole lives an act of worship, not just what happens at a service. He warns them not to let the surrounding culture decide who they are or what they value. Instead, he says, let your mind be renewed so you can figure out what is actually good.

reflection.reflection: Paul says our everyday lives, not just our big moments, are where real transformation happens. Small choices add up and gradually shape who we become.
reflection.question: Think about one habit you have on a regular weekday. Does it tend to leave you feeling more like the person you want to be, or less?

readings.label: Gospel
readings.fullText:
Jesus began to show his disciples
that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer greatly
from the elders, the chief priests, and the scribes,
and be killed and on the third day be raised.
Then Peter took Jesus aside and began to rebuke him,
"God forbid, Lord! No such thing shall ever happen to you."
He turned and said to Peter,
"Get behind me, Satan! You are an obstacle to me.
You are thinking not as God does, but as human beings do."

Then Jesus said to his disciples,
"Whoever wishes to come after me must deny himself,
take up his cross, and follow me.
For whoever wishes to save his life will lose it,
but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it.
What profit would there be for one to gain the whole world
and forfeit his life?
Or what can one give in exchange for his life?
For the Son of Man will come with his angels in his Father's glory,
and then he will repay all according to his conduct."
readings.summary: Jesus tells his disciples plainly that he is going to suffer and die in Jerusalem. Peter pulls him aside and pushes back hard. He doesn't want that for Jesus. But Jesus corrects him sharply, because Peter is thinking about what feels safe, not what is true. Then Jesus turns to all of them and says that following him means picking up your own cross, not avoiding it.

reflection.reflection: Jesus does not promise an easy road. He promises that the things worth having often require us to let go of what feels safe or comfortable.
reflection.question: Is there something in your life right now that you know is worth doing but that you've been putting off because it feels hard or risky?
